What it means for the dark-matter numbers. In the stellar frame the dark-matter cloud is cut and scaled by the stars' size, and the encoder uses that size. The stellar-frame dark-matter results of Section 6.6 therefore contain information the cloud inherits from the stars, most visibly the stellar size and, through it, part of the stellar mass. The halo-frame run is the fairer measure of the dark matter's own information, though Rvmax still depends on the total mass, stars included: mean R² 0.52 against 0.40 for statistics of the same clouds, and stars–dark matter R@1 of 10.7%, 46 times chance. Dark-matter mass, black-hole mass and stellar metallicity are predicted equally well in both frames.

A side result on data size. 20% fewer training galaxies cost only 0.7 points of mean R@1 (37.7% → 37.0%) and 1.2 points of stars–dark matter R@1, less than the 2.5 points between two seeds of the final setup. In this range the number of training galaxies matters little for the PointNet. Both controls ran with one seed: the frame effect (8.1 points of stars–dark matter R@1, 0.26 of half-mass-radius R²) lies well outside the seed spread, the training-set effect does not.

c30_notes: This run separates the two changes of the halo-frame control. It trains the final setup in the normal stellar frame, but only on the 3,252 galaxies the halo-frame run could use, and scores it on the same 428 frozen validation galaxies. The answer is clear: it lands next to the final setup, not next to the halo-frame run. Stars to dark matter retrieval is 18.8%, against 20.0% for the final setup and 10.7% in the halo frame. The dark-matter embedding predicts stellar mass with R squared 0.78, against 0.79 and 0.68, and the half-mass radius with 0.71, against 0.72 and 0.45. So the frame causes the drop, not the smaller training set: the stellar frame hands the dark-matter cloud the stars' size, and part of the dark-matter result came from that. The halo-frame numbers are the fairer measure of what the dark matter carries itself, and there the embedding still beats statistics of the same clouds, 0.52 against 0.40 mean R squared. A side result: 20% fewer training galaxies cost only 0.7 points of mean R@1. Each control ran with one seed, but the frame effect of about 8 points is well outside the seed spread of about 2.5 points.
